title: Bendigo Bank to pay APRA penalty
full_text:
The prudential regulator will penalise Bendigo Bank $8m over shortcomings in the regional lender’s cyber security and systemic protections designed to protect the financial system from rogue actors.
Bendigo Bank had agreed to a penalty deal with the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, with the terms made public late on Monday after questions from The Australian.
An APRA spokesman on Monday said the regulator is “making an announcement tomorrow morning and we have nothing to disclose until then”.
Bendigo Bank said it had agreed to the fine from APRA over breaches of the Banking Act between 2020 and 2023. The bank will also book $2.6m in court costs from the matter.
The penalty relates to Bendigo Bank’s former Alliance Bank business, which was closed in September 2024. The Alliance Bank suffered a major cyber leak in March 2023, with 250 accounts compromised and $140,000 misappropriated. Bendigo Bank boss Richard Fennell said customers “can be assured that once identified, we acted immediately to address the issue, and made sure all impacted customers were fully reimbursed.” Sources told The Australian the deal between Bendigo Bank and APRA comes after months of concerns within the regulator over the bank, which is already a regulatory target over its vulnerability to money laundering.
These sources said the imminent deal concerns Bendigo Bank’s technology and cyber security readiness.
Last year, APRA and Austrac, the regulator charged with stopping money laundering, slugged Bendigo Bank with orders to hold an extra $50m in capital after finding it had weak risk management and identification, mitigation, and management of terror financing and money laundering.
Bendigo Bank in turn announced it would commission a review of its systems, to be run by consulting firm Deloitte.
The newest iteration of orders to be signed off by a court comes as Bendigo Bank has been scrambling to uplift its technology systems, inking a multi-year deal with Google to use its AI systems, as well as implementing an outsourcing plan with Infosys and Genpact.
Around 80 per cent of 188 technology staff at Bendigo Bank who are set to go under an outsourcing plan have been offered jobs at consulting firm Infosys. However, around 30 staff have not.
Mr Fennell previously said the changes would improve the lender’s technology. “With this access to Infosys’ global capabilities, software engineering and AI talent, our bank has greater capacity to innovate,” Mr Fennell said. “These necessary changes create clearer accountability.”
